title: Mina and Bram's Big Storm
markdown:
Mina the goat, lighthouse helper, adjusted her woollen scarf. The market square buzzed with colour and sound, but today was more than market day. It was judging day. Inspector Grimshaw, a man whose waistcoat seemed to hold secrets, was due any moment. Mina wanted everything just so. She pictured herself explaining foghorn calibration with a confident bleat.

Beside her, Bram the stoat, her lab partner, meticulously polished a brass barometer. Bram was quieter, watchful. He noticed the wind’s unusual whisper and the gulls circling lower. He scribbled a quick note.

“Mina,” he murmured, “the wind meter showed a sudden jump. And look towards the eastern docks. The sky has a peculiar bruised hue.”

Mina, busy arranging charts, waved a hoof. “Oh, Bram, please, not now. Inspector Grimshaw is here. It’s all about presentation. Looking the part.” She practised a serene smile. Nerves fluttered anyway.

Inspector Grimshaw arrived, smelling faintly of pipe tobacco. “Ah, Miss Mina,” he boomed, “I hear remarkable things about the lighthouse’s efficiency.”

Mina beamed. Her moment. She launched into a speech about coastal erosion. Bram kept his gaze on the horizon. He nudged a small wooden boat on Mina’s table. “Mina,” he insisted gently, “this boat is listing. The tide is pulling it unexpectedly.”

The inspector was captivated by Mina’s delivery. “Fascinating,” he murmured. He had not noticed the darkening sky or the unnatural stillness of the seabirds.

Then a mighty gust swept the square. Awnings billowed. Things tumbled. Paper lanterns swayed violently. Pleasant market scents thickened with the sharp tang of an approaching storm. The familiar square transformed.

Mina gasped. Composure shattered. Spectacles slipped. She had focused so hard on seeming an expert that she had missed the actual signs. The inspector clutched his waistcoat. “Oh dear,” he stammered.

It was Bram, the quiet observer, who sprang. “The storm’s moving in faster than predicted,” he announced, voice steady. “The seawall needs immediate reinforcement. And we must secure those lanterns.” He pointed to a loose support beam on a market stall, a detail Mina had not registered.

Mina, for the first time, truly saw Bram: quiet competence, genuine concern. The rehearsed performance felt hollow. “You’re right, Bram!” She dropped her charts. “Let’s secure the seawall!”

With a shared glance they worked. Mina braced stalls, hooves finding purchase. Bram darted among vendors, quick precise instructions. He pointed out weak spots. She secured them with urgency. The inspector watched, a slow smile of admiration.

As the first fat raindrops drummed, the market was safe. The inspector cleared his throat. “Well now. It seems the most valuable helper was the one I hadn’t been paying sufficient attention to. Excellent work, Mr. Bram. Your observations were invaluable.”

Mina felt a warmth spread, quiet pride in something important done together. She looked at Bram, fur ruffled and damp. They did not need a speech about listening. They stood side by side, looking out at the now-secure harbour, scarves and whiskers equally wet, while the storm rumbled itself to a close and the barometer, at last, had something honest to say.
characters: Mina (a goat lighthouse helper), Bram (the stoat lab partner)
